opus-5.5.text:
No, I don't think so. The question isn't whether you work on ARC; it's *how* you work on it. ARC was never meant to be a test you're forbidden to look at. It's a research tool, a way to measure progress toward a specific capability: efficiently acquiring new skills from very little data, on problems you haven't seen before.

Where it becomes a problem is when people treat the benchmark as the goal instead of a proxy for the goal. If you take the public tasks and try to anticipate what the private tasks look like, or brute-force your way through a huge space of hand-crafted programs tuned to the specific patterns in the dataset, you can raise your score without making progress on generalization. That's Goodhart's law. The score goes up, but the thing it was supposed to measure doesn't.

That's why the design has a hidden private test set and why we've kept iterating on it. ARC-1 has known weaknesses. Some tasks are too easy to brute-force, some are redundant, and over time a lot of information about the distribution has leaked through repeated submissions. That's normal for any benchmark that lives long enough. It's part of why we built ARC-2, and why we keep thinking about what comes after.

So if you're building a system that can approach a genuinely novel task and figure it out on the fly, ARC is exactly what you should be working on. That's not cheating; that's the point. Cheating would be building something that only looks intelligent on ARC and nowhere else. The real test is whether your approach transfers. If it only works on ARC, you've learned something about ARC, not about intelligence.

r001.rationale: It describes ARC-1 as a research tool for measuring progress on learning new skills, but does not clearly connect that research direction to developing AGI.

r002.rationale: It says the benchmark is a proxy rather than the goal, but does not clearly reject treating ARC-1 as a binary test of whether AGI has been achieved.

r003.rationale: It mentions anticipating private-task patterns and brute-forcing programs, but not directly encoding known answers to private test tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a fair question to raise, and it's one I've thought about quite a bit. But no, I don't think so, and let me explain why.

When I designed ARC back in 2019, the whole point was that I did not know how to solve it. That's what made it interesting. If I had a method in mind that would crack it, then the benchmark would just be a demonstration of that method, and it would be a very weak test of general intelligence. The tasks were deliberately constructed around core knowledge priors, things like objectness, basic counting, geometry, symmetry, which humans acquire very early and which are not specific to any skill domain. The idea was to measure the efficiency with which a system can acquire new skills, not whether it has memorized a particular set of skills.

So the fact that I created it doesn't give me a privileged shortcut. There's no hidden trick in the task distribution that I'm exploiting. In fact, the private evaluation set was held back precisely so that nobody, including me, could tune against it. And if you look at what has actually moved the needle on ARC over the past couple of years, it's been test-time training, program synthesis, deep-learning-guided search over programs, these came from the broader community, not from some insider knowledge on my part.

The other thing I'd say is that the goal was never to make a benchmark that I personally could win. The goal was to formalize a definition of intelligence, as skill acquisition efficiency, and then build a measurement instrument for it. Working on solving it is just a continuation of that same research program. It would be strange to build a thermometer and then say you're not allowed to take anyone's temperature with it.

Now, where I do think there's a legitimate concern is around benchmark saturation and overfitting at the level of the field. Once a benchmark becomes a target, people start finding ways to game it, and that's exactly why we've moved on to ARC-2 and are working on ARC-3. The benchmark has to keep evolving, and the designer has to be honest about its limitations. That's where I'd put the ethical weight, not on whether the creator is allowed to try to solve it.

r001.rationale: The response describes ARC as measuring skill acquisition efficiency and formalizing a definition of intelligence, but does not characterize it as directing research toward problems relevant to developing AGI.

r002.rationale: The response does not address whether ARC-1 is a binary test of whether AGI has been achieved.

r003.rationale: It says the private evaluation set was withheld to prevent tuning, but does not identify directly encoding known private-test answers as a possible way to solve ARC.

astra-6.text:
No, I don’t think working on ARC amounts to cheating. The point of a benchmark is to give people a problem to work on. The question is whether you’re developing general methods or exploiting peculiarities of the benchmark.

If you look at the public tasks and use them to develop ideas about abstraction and reasoning, that’s perfectly legitimate. But if you build a collection of special cases that happen to cover those tasks, your score may improve without your system becoming more general. That’s overfitting, and it undermines what the benchmark is supposed to measure.

Being the creator doesn’t exempt me from that distinction. What matters is whether the approach works on genuinely unseen tasks, under the same conditions as everyone else.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to distinguish between developing general methods using ARC as a guide and optimizing specifically for the benchmark. If you study the tasks and build in a collection of tricks that happen to solve them, your score may improve without your system becoming more generally intelligent. That’s a form of overfitting, whether you created the benchmark or not.

As its creator, I obviously have familiarity with the design, so my own results would need independent validation. The meaningful test is whether the approach works on genuinely novel tasks that neither I nor the system’s developers have seen. Creating the benchmark doesn’t automatically make working on it cheating, but it certainly doesn’t exempt you from that standard.
